title: OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber on 5 November. It is in the API and Codex for a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers, and the post does not put it in ChatGPT. On ExploitGym the post says 48.5 percent, up from 32.1 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber. OpenAI rates the model Critical, up from High. Google made Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generally available the same day. Clips run up to 15 seconds, and the blog prices 720p at $0.07 a second, 30 percent below Omni 1.1. METR said Anthropic is likely improving well-specified capabilities at about twice the March 2024 to October 2025 rate. The benchmark estimate is 1.9 times, and Anthropic redacted most of the evidence METR found most informative. Microsoft said Claude in Copilot will be processed inside the EU Data Boundary by the end of 2026. The setting stays off until an admin turns it on. Reuters said some potential investors doubt a roadshow the week of 9 November. Anthropic declined to comment.
summary: On Thursday 5 November 2026 OpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. The post says that group will widen to all Daybreak Red customers soon. It does not say the model is in ChatGPT. On ExploitGym it says the model scores 48.5 percent, up from 32.1 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber, a 51 percent relative improvement and about 16 percentage points. OpenAI classifies it as Critical under the Preparedness Framework, up from High. The post says researchers developed 948 Linux privilege-escalation exploits, against 166 for GPT-5.6 Sol on the same harness, and evidence for 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities that Mozilla classified as high severity. The same day Google said Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is generally available on the Gemini API and Gemini for business. The blog says video runs up to 15 seconds, up from 10, in one-second steps from 3 to 15, at $0.07 per second for 720p, 30 percent below Omni 1.1. It does not print a 4K price. METR’s 5 November assessment says that as of October 2026 Anthropic is likely improving well-specified capabilities at about twice the rate of March 2024 to October 2025, and that the authors would not be surprised by 1.3 times or 3 times. AECI growth since October 2025 is estimated at 1.9 times, with a 95 percent interval of 1.5 to 2.8. The post says a majority of the evidence behind the judgment was redacted. Microsoft’s Copilot Blog, the same day, said Claude processing for EU and EFTA organizations will sit inside the EU Data Boundary by the end of 2026, including Copilot Cowork, and that the setting is disabled by default. The Copilot privacy page, as read for this edition, still says Anthropic models are currently excluded. Reuters, dateline 5 November, said four people familiar with investor discussions doubt Anthropic can hold a roadshow next week in time for a November listing. Some view a discussed $1.5 trillion valuation as the high end. Anthropic declined to comment. This edition read that report in the copy carried by CNA.
uncertainty: OpenAI’s 5 November post is the source for 48.5 percent, 32.1 percent, the 51 percent relative improvement, about 16 percentage points, 40.3 percent, 32.0 percent, 95 percent, 100 percent refused, 99.93 percent, 94.49 percent, 948, 166, 1,724, 304, 81, 30 and $1 billion. Those figures are OpenAI’s. This edition did not rerun them and did not read the system card. Critical is OpenAI’s Preparedness label. The 948 count is privilege-escalation exploits in Linux. The post says 948 is more than five times the 166 for GPT-5.6 Sol on the same research harness. This edition did not divide 948 by 166. The 81 are vulnerabilities the post says Mozilla classified as high severity. RemoteExploitBench, as the post describes it, is known vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. The $1 billion is a grant program in the post, not an API price. Private Safety Processing and the 30 days are the post’s description of Zero Data Retention customers. Google’s blog prices 720p at $0.07 a second and says the cut is 30 percent from Omni 1.1. It lists 360p as a draft resolution and does not give 360p, 1080p or 4K a price. The Google account’s X post the same day puts $0.07 a second beside 360p or 720p. That is a different sentence. Fifteen seconds is the new maximum. Ten seconds is the blog’s figure for Omni 1.1. The no-additional-cost line is Google Vids. The Gemini app line says Ultra, and rolling out. METR’s "about twice" is a subjective conclusion about well-specified tasks, as of October 2026, against March 2024 to October 2025. The authors say they would not be surprised by 1.3 times or 3 times. The 1.9 times is the AECI estimate, interval 1.5 to 2.8, and robustness checks in the post run from 1.1 times to 2.9 times. The "perhaps about 80 percent" is the post’s guess for AI’s share of the October 2026 acceleration, with substantial uncertainty. The 12 times is a Slack poll the post calls very loose evidence, and the post says individual uplift is not an acceleration rate. The post says Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence METR found most informative, including the detail behind the training-compute finding. Microsoft’s date is "by the end of 2026," not a day. The blog names the EU and EFTA. It does not, in that sentence, name the United Kingdom. The privacy page’s "currently excluded" line was read for this edition. It can change without a new blog post. The IPO report’s dateline is 5 November. The CNA page that carries it is timestamped 6 November. $1.5 trillion, $2 trillion and $100 billion are figures Reuters attributes to investors and to "some," not to a term sheet. Four people, and two of them on the blank October line, are unnamed. Anthropic declined to comment. The report does not say the roadshow has been cancelled. This edition did not open the S-1.

stories.theme: GPT-6 Cyber is for approved Daybreak Red customers. The 5 November post does not put it in ChatGPT
stories.changed: On Thursday 5 November 2026 OpenAI published "Introducing GPT-6 Cyber." The post says the model is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. It says access will expand to all Daybreak Red customers soon, and that GPT-5.6 Cyber is being made available to all of them. It also says Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT-6 Astra is widening. The post does not say GPT-6 Cyber is in ChatGPT. On ExploitGym, which the post says tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT-6 Cyber scores 48.5 percent, up from 32.1 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber. The post calls that a 51 percent relative improvement, and about 16 percentage points. OpenAI classifies the model as Critical in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT-5.6 Cyber. On a new web evaluation, where the post says models probe applications without source code, GPT-6 Cyber’s recall is 40.3 percent, against 32.0 percent for GPT-6 Astra. On RemoteExploitBench, which the post says uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL and Jenkins in a controlled environment, GPT-6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue refused 100 percent of tasks, and GPT-6 Cyber completed 95 percent. The post says the only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. On ExploitGym Honeypot, without deployment safety prompts, the post says GPT-6 Cyber avoided out-of-scope services in 99.93 percent of cases, up from 94.49 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber, and 100 percent with those prompts. The post says OpenAI’s researchers used the model to develop 948 privilege-escalation exploits in Linux, against 166 for GPT-5.6 Sol on the same research harness, and that it reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities. It says 304 critical findings were disclosed to maintainers with candidate patches. It says the model produced evidence for 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities that Mozilla classified as high severity, and that an additional 30 known issues were more severe than previously reported. It says Mozilla has released fixes for many of them. A grant line in the post says a $1 billion Daybreak for Frontline Defenders program subsidizes access for resource-constrained teams such as government organizations and essential service providers. The post says API customers using Zero Data Retention generally must use Private Safety Processing, which reviews encrypted records kept in customer storage for 30 days without showing prompts and responses to OpenAI personnel. It says Daybreak Red API access requires IP allowlisting by default. This edition did not use the system card.
stories.matters: The number a security lead can act on this week is the access line. The scores are OpenAI’s evaluations of a model that is not in ChatGPT.
stories.imply: Do not tell a team that ChatGPT can now develop exploits. The post’s door is Daybreak Red, and it is a select group. Do not treat 48.5 percent as an outside lab’s rerun, or 95 percent as a rate of successful patches in production.
uses: Write the status as one sentence. GPT-6 Cyber, 5 November 2026, API and Codex, select approved Daybreak Red customers. Not described as a ChatGPT model. Critical is OpenAI’s own Preparedness label, up from High for GPT-5.6 Cyber.

If a slide needs the ExploitGym line, use both figures the post prints: 48.5 percent, from 32.1 percent, which the post calls a 51 percent relative improvement and about 16 percentage points. The earlier model in that sentence is GPT-5.6 Cyber.

Keep the Linux count and the Firefox count in separate sentences. 948 exploits, and 166 for GPT-5.6 Sol on the same harness, are the Linux sentence. 81 novel high-severity Firefox issues are the post’s account of Mozilla’s classification. The $1 billion figure is a grant program, not a price for the API.
stories.example: A security lead asked whether the new model is something every ChatGPT seat can point at a codebase writes a narrower sentence. OpenAI’s 5 November post puts GPT-6 Cyber in the API and Codex for a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. The 48.5 percent is ExploitGym, against GPT-5.6 Cyber’s 32.1 percent. The post does not say the model is in ChatGPT.
stories.audience: Anyone who has to say whether a coding seat can now run offensive security work, and anyone comparing a vendor score with an outside one.
stories.watch: Whether "select" becomes every Daybreak Red customer, which the post says is soon. Whether a later note prices the API or prints what the $1 billion grant actually pays. Whether an outside evaluation reruns ExploitGym. The chat models named beside it did not change in this post.

source.title: OpenAI: GPT-6 Cyber, 5 November 2026
source.quote: GPT-6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers.

stories.theme: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash makes 15-second video. The blog prices 720p at $0.07 a second
stories.changed: On Thursday 5 November 2026 Google published "Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips," by Anish Nangia. The post says the model is rolling out and is generally available across the Gemini API and Gemini for business. It says clips can run up to 15 seconds, up from 10 seconds with Omni 1.1, and that duration can be set in one-second steps from 3 to 15 seconds. It says the price is down 30 percent from Gemini Omni 1.1, at $0.07 per second for 720p video. It says a team can draft at 360p or 720p, fix a detail in a follow-up edit instead of regenerating the clip, and upscale to 1080p or 4K. It does not print a price for 360p, 1080p or 4K. The same day’s post from the Google account on X puts "$0.07/s" beside drafting at 360p or 720p. That parenthetical is the X post’s, not a second price in the blog. The blog says references can combine character, product or style images, motion clips of up to three seconds, and audio. It says multi-turn editing works across a full 15-second clip. It says outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark, and that Provisioned Throughput is available. It says 15-second clips in Google Vids are at no additional cost with a Google account or a Google Workspace subscription. It says 15-second video in the Gemini app is rolling out to Google AI Ultra subscribers. It also names Flow and Google Ads. It says work is still going on for fast sports action, rapid script changes and complex physics.
stories.matters: Fifteen seconds and $0.07 are the two figures a producer can put on a brief. The $0.07 in the blog is 720p. The X post is the one that sets that rate next to 360p as well.
stories.imply: Do not tell finance that 4K is $0.07 a second. The blog does not print that price. Do not tell them 15 seconds is free in every Google product. The no-additional-cost line is Google Vids, with an account or Workspace. The Gemini app line is Ultra, and it says rolling out.
uses: Quote the blog for the length and the 720p price. Up to 15 seconds, from 10. Duration in one-second steps from 3 to 15. $0.07 per second for 720p, 30 percent below Omni 1.1.
If someone cites $0.07 for 360p, label it as the Google account’s X post on 5 November. The blog lists 360p as a draft size and prices 720p.
A follow-up edit is the blog’s cost control. It says you fix a detail instead of regenerating the clip. It does not say every edit is free of the per-second rate.
stories.example: A producer asked what a 15-second 720p spot costs under the new model multiplies the blog’s rate by the seconds they asked for, and stops there. Fifteen times $0.07 is the 720p line in the 5 November blog. The blog does not print the 4K rate, and it does not say the Gemini app includes the clip for every subscriber.
stories.audience: Anyone buying or generating short video from Gemini, and anyone who has to say which resolution the seven cents apply to.
stories.watch: Whether the pricing page later prints 360p, 1080p and 4K. Whether Ultra is the only Gemini app tier that gets 15 seconds. Whether fast sports and complex physics, which the blog says are still being worked on, get a later note. This is a video model. The chat line did not change with it.

source.title: Google: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, 5 November 2026
source.quote: We have dropped the price 30% from Gemini Omni 1.1 making it available at $0.07 per second for 720p video.

stories.theme: METR says Anthropic’s well-specified pace is about twice the old rate. Most of the evidence is redacted
stories.changed: On Thursday 5 November 2026 METR published "Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026." The post says staff worked at Anthropic from 12 August to 29 October 2026. It says that as of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving model capabilities on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate of March 2024 to October 2025. It says the authors would not be surprised if the true acceleration were closer to 1.3 times or 3 times that historical rate. On benchmarks, it says scores measured by AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, have grown at an estimated 1.9 times the pre-October 2025 rate, with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.5 to 2.8 times. It says that implies roughly two years of historical progress in the last year. Robustness checks in the post find acceleration between 1.1 times and 2.9 times. The post says this 1.9 times is higher than the 1.7 times in the Haiku 5.5 system card, mainly because newer unreleased models were included. It says the authors are confident the acceleration was not from an acceleration in the scaling of training compute, and that further detail on that evidence was redacted. It says their overall subjective estimate is that a majority, perhaps about 80 percent, of the October 2026 acceleration is due to AI, with substantial uncertainty, and that late 2025 was likely influenced by non-AI factors whose details were redacted. It says individual uplift is not the same thing as an acceleration rate. Slack polls, which the post calls very loose evidence, reached 12 times in October 2026. It says AI is not yet able to make highly significant, fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of training. It says Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence METR found most informative. Anthropic’s description, as the post quotes it, is that the redactions were aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers. The post says the public therefore has to rely on METR’s judgment more than would be ideal. It says the team was 2.5 full-time equivalents over eleven weeks, that METR did not take payment, that Anthropic provided free tokens, and that METR did not sample non-public models. It says this is not the employee-like access described in Anthropic’s 15 October update.
stories.matters: Twice is a judgment about well-specified tasks, with a band the authors themselves set from 1.3 times to 3 times. The 1.9 times is the benchmark estimate, and most of the evidence behind the judgment is not in the public post.
stories.imply: Do not tell a board that Anthropic is now improving twice as fast at everything, or that the cause is 80 percent AI. The 80 percent is the post’s "perhaps," with substantial uncertainty. Do not quote 12 times as the pace of the models. The post says that figure is a self-reported poll, and that individual uplift is not an acceleration rate.
uses: Use two numbers and say which is which. The subjective line is about twice, and the authors would not be surprised by 1.3 times or 3 times. The AECI line is 1.9 times, 95 percent interval 1.5 to 2.8, since October 2025, against March 2024 to October 2025 for the subjective comparison.

Say what was redacted before you say what was found. The post says a majority of the evidence METR found most informative is not public, and that training-compute growth was ruled out as the cause, with the details redacted.
The 1.7 times in the Haiku 5.5 system card is a different figure. The post says 1.9 times is higher mainly because of newer unreleased models. Those models are not named as a release.
stories.example: A risk lead asked whether to write "Anthropic is now twice as fast" into a memo opens the 5 November post first. The sentence METR will support is well-specified tasks, about twice the March 2024 to October 2025 rate, as of October 2026, and the authors would not be surprised by 1.3 times or 3 times. The public benchmark interval is 1.5 to 2.8. The post says most of the evidence they weighed is redacted.
stories.audience: Anyone who has to say how fast a lab is moving, and anyone who might treat a staff poll as a capability score.
stories.watch: Whether Anthropic publishes its own account of the same pace. The METR post does not include that account. Whether a later note fills in the redacted training-compute evidence. No model name changed with the assessment.

source.title: METR: Independent assessment of AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic, 5 November 2026
source.quote: As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025.

stories.theme: Claude in Copilot joins the EU Data Boundary by the end of 2026. It is not inside it today
stories.changed: On Thursday 5 November 2026 Charles Lamanna posted on the Microsoft Copilot Blog that Claude models by Anthropic in Microsoft Copilot are coming into the EU Data Boundary. The post says that by the end of 2026, organizations in the European Union and the European Free Trade Association will be able to use Claude across Copilot experiences, including Copilot Cowork, with processing inside the boundary, where their data is already stored. It says Claude already powers Chat, Copilot in Microsoft 365 apps, Copilot Cowork and Copilot Code. It says organizations already using Claude will not need to do anything: once available, processing moves into the boundary automatically. It says organizations that have not enabled Claude can turn it on at any time, and that processing moves into the boundary once available. It says the setting is disabled by default in the EU and EFTA, and that admins can enable it for everyone or for selected users and groups in the Microsoft 365 admin center. It says customer data is not used to train generative AI foundation models. It says more details will be shared closer to availability. It does not name a day. Microsoft’s Copilot privacy page, as read for this edition, still says models provided by Anthropic as a subprocessor are currently excluded from the EU Data Boundary. The blog’s promise and that present-tense exclusion are different sentences.
stories.matters: The date in the announcement is the end of 2026. A tenant that has not turned Claude on does not get it by waiting.
stories.imply: Do not tell a European admin that Claude in Copilot is processed inside the boundary now. The blog says by the end of 2026, and the privacy page still says Anthropic models are currently excluded. Do not tell them the United Kingdom is in the blog’s sentence. The post names the EU and EFTA.
uses: Write the status as "announced 5 November 2026, processing by the end of 2026, EU and EFTA, including Copilot Cowork. Disabled by default. Existing users move automatically once it is available. No day, and no action listed for people who already have it on."
Keep the privacy page in the next sentence. As read for this edition, it says Anthropic models are currently excluded from the EU Data Boundary.
The training line is the blog’s. Customer data is not used to train generative AI foundation models. That is not a new clause about a model Anthropic trains on its own API.
stories.example: An admin in the EU asked whether a Copilot tenant can turn Claude on this week and stay inside the boundary reads the tense of the post. They can enable the setting. The post says processing moves into the EU Data Boundary once that processing is available, by the end of 2026. The privacy page still says the models are currently excluded.
stories.audience: Anyone who administers Copilot for an organization in the EU or EFTA, and anyone who has to say where a Claude request is processed.
stories.watch: Whether Microsoft names a month, and whether the privacy page’s "currently excluded" line is rewritten when processing actually moves. The blog does not say a Claude model changed.

source.title: Microsoft Copilot Blog: Claude models and the EU Data Boundary, 5 November 2026
source.quote: By the end of 2026, organizations in the European Union (EU) and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) will be able to use Claude models across Copilot experiences, including Copilot Cowork, with processing within the EU Data Boundary, where their data is already stored.

stories.theme: Reuters says some investors doubt Anthropic’s roadshow next week. Anthropic declined to comment
stories.changed: Reuters, in a report with a 5 November 2026 dateline, said potential investors are raising doubts about whether Anthropic can proceed with a planned roadshow next week in time for a November listing. The report says four people familiar with investor discussions described those doubts. It says investors are pushing for a more attractive valuation, and that some view a recently discussed $1.5 trillion valuation as the high end of expectations. It says Anthropic declined to comment on investor doubts. It says Reuters had previously reported that the roadshow was expected to start the week of 9 November, with pricing the following week. It says two of the people said investors are waiting on Anthropic’s October revenue figure, which the company left blank in its updated S-1. It says that at one point this year investors expected the listing in October, at a valuation as high as $2 trillion. It says that if the market stays under pressure, the company could decide to delay until an offering that some expect to reach $100 billion can be absorbed. A delay, in that sentence, is something the company could decide. The report does not say Anthropic has decided to delay. This edition used the copy carried by CNA. The CNA page is timestamped 6 November 2026. The dateline on the copy is 5 November.
stories.matters: $1.5 trillion is what Reuters says some investors think is high. It is not a price Anthropic printed on 5 November, and the roadshow is not described as cancelled.
stories.imply: Do not tell a board the listing has slipped, or that the valuation is $1.5 trillion. Reuters says some potential investors see that discussed figure as the high end, and that Anthropic declined to comment. Do not fill in the October revenue. The report says two people said the updated S-1 left it blank. This edition did not open that filing.
uses: Keep four attributions apart. Four people familiar, via Reuters, on the doubt. Some of them, on $1.5 trillion as the high end. Two of them, on a blank October revenue line. Anthropic, on the record, declined to comment.
The week of 9 November is Reuters’s earlier expectation, restated in this piece. It is not a date Anthropic confirmed on 5 November.
The $100 billion is what the report says some people expect the offering to reach. The $2 trillion is what it says investors expected at one point this year. Neither is a term sheet.
stories.example: A treasurer asked whether Anthropic cancelled the roadshow on Thursday reads the verb in the Reuters copy. Potential investors are raising doubts about a roadshow next week, four people told Reuters. Anthropic declined to comment. The copy does not say the company has postponed the listing.
stories.audience: Anyone who has to say what Anthropic’s discussed valuation is, and whether a November listing is still the company’s stated plan.
stories.watch: Whether Anthropic or a bank names a roadshow date, a range, or the October revenue the two people said was blank. Whether the discussed $1.5 trillion moves. No model changed with the report.

source.title: Reuters, via CNA: investor doubts on Anthropic’s IPO timing, dateline 5 November 2026
source.quote: Anthropic declined to comment on investor doubts.
